name: Kanakanavu
confidence_why: Cheng 2020, Cheng 2023, Wild 2018, Sung 2018, Chen 2016 and Sung 1966 all place default prominence on the penultimate syllable with predictable final and antepenultimate exceptions; the only disagreement is Cheng 2023's own recasting of the 2020 weight-based rule as underlying-vowel counting, which changes the mechanism but not where stress falls, while Tsuchida 2003's claim that stress is phonemic rests on a few minimal pairs of very low functional load that the later analyses treat as lexical exceptions.

catalog_quote: In this study, the realization of prosodic prominence is deemed “mostly predictable” (ibid. 83) as it can be attributed to (i) regular prominence realization on the underlying penultimate mora of a word, and to (ii) phonological factors that result in deviations from the regular penultimate position. [...] One phonological factor that productively results in deviation from the regular penultimate prominence pattern is syllable weight in word-final position. Words that contain underlyingly final heavy syllables, including native and loan words, are found to have prominence realized on the final syllable, which contains the penultimate mora in the underlying representation [...] In addition, we agree with H. Chen (2016) in deeming that the location of prominence is predictable, and that there are divergences from the regular penultimate pattern that can be related to interaction with other phonological processes or the underlying representation of the forms in question. [...] Although the surface prominence-realizing unit is the syllable (the prototypical stress-bearing unit), it is clearly the mora (the prototypical tone-bearing unit) that is the de facto prominence-bearing unit, as it has been repetitively demonstrated that identifying the underlyingly penultimate mora predicts surface realization of prominence.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence (traditionally 'stress', realized as a high pitch target plus longer duration) falls on the syllable containing the underlyingly penultimate mora: the penultimate syllable in ordinary (CV)nCVCV words; the final syllable when it is underlyingly heavy (VV, including heavy finals created by vowel-initial suffixes, and CVN finals arising from loss of a post-nasal final high vowel); the antepenultimate syllable when the word ends in an extrametrical echo vowel (vutúkuru 'fish'). Prefixes do not move it; suffixation recomputes it (rightward shift). A small lexically specified class bears a falling HL prominence that is always penultimate, and a few affixes are prominence-attracting or -repelling. Every content word has exactly one prominence (obligatory, culminative).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Cheng 2020: no word considered 'unequivocally show[s] more than one prosodically prominent syllable' (p. 44); H. Chen 2016 reportedly discusses the 'possibility of secondary stress' (not seen). Sung 1966: in words of four or more syllables pitch rises from the second syllable to the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically specified HL-prominence words (e.g. umâra 'take (AV)', makâsi, kajsîsi) invariably penultimate regardless of structure; prominence-attracting suffix -an gives invariable final prominence; loans with final long vowels (punéː 'pigeon') final; older sources (Tsuchida 1976/2003, Sung 1966 implicitly, Li 2026) call stress phonemically distinctive with very low functional load, citing pairs like nipapacé'era 'showed' vs nipapace'éra 'looked at each other' and man'man 'like' vs 'manman 'chili' (S. Chen 2015); Wild 2018 and H. Chen 2016 found no evidence of distinctiveness.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (content words in citation form and in connected speech transcriptions); Tsuchida 2003 notes stress position shifts when particles precede/follow and that in excited narration a sentence-initial strong high-pitched stress can flatten other word stresses (phrase-level intonation). Cheng treats the mora as the prominence-bearing unit and the surface syllable as the realizing unit; he deliberately avoids classifying the system as 'stress' vs 'pitch accent' (property-driven: privative /H, HL, Ø/ on the penultimate mora).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single surviving Kanakanavu speech community (Takanua/Dakanua and Minquan villages, Namasia District, Kaohsiung); no dialect split relevant to stress. Glottolog kana1286 = ISO xnb. Note the older (Sung 1966, Tsuchida 1976/2003) vs. recent (Wild 2018, H. Chen 2016, Cheng 2020) descriptions differ on whether stress is phonemic: older work calls it distinctive with very low functional load; recent work treats position as predictable from moraic structure plus a small lexically specified HL class.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every open-class content word has exactly one prosodically prominent syllable (culminative, privative), realised mainly by a high pitch target (plus length and intensity when not penultimate). Prominence is assigned by counting underlying vowels: by default it goes on the penultimate underlying vowel; it goes on the antepenultimate underlying vowel only when the unsuffixed word has exactly four underlying vowels. Because underlying vowel sequences coalesce or form glides and final/medial high vowels drop (apocope, syncope) after prominence is assigned, the surface position may be penult (57% of 241 verbs, e.g. mukúsa 'go'), antepenult (~21%, e.g. mókusa, vutúkulu 'fish') or final (~21%, e.g. ukusún, mukusá 'go (imp)'). The author states this is not weight-sensitive (p. 73), contrasting it with Bunun and Paiwan. p. 43: 'Word-prosodic prominence in Kanakanavu may be realized on the penultimate, final or antepenultimate surface syllable of a word.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'every content word shows at least one and at most one syllable that is prosodically prominent' (p. 43); fn. 10 characterises it as privative and culminative in Hyman's (2009) terms. In discourse an emphatic utterance-level prominence (marked with a circumflex) may be overlaid on, or replace, word-level prominence on the first content word of an intonation unit (pp. 85-86).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Unsuffixed words with exactly four underlying vowels take antepenultimate prominence (p. 47; e.g. pókali /poo-kali/, kumóru /k<um>ooru/). (ii) Prominence assignment is ordered before apocope and syncope, so navúngu ~ navúng shows penult ~ final, and syncopated four-vowel words end with antepenult prominence (vántuku 'money', mánman 'children'), pp. 73-78. (iii) Prominence-specified morphemes (pp. 78-83): a few stems with invariable antepenultimate prominence (savúana 'medicine', matú'usu 'encounter'), full CVCV reduplication and fossilised reduplicated forms with invariable antepenult (manúmanu 'children', 'aná'ana 'cosmos'), and two prominence-attracting suffixes, readers-voice mild imperative -án and patient-voice mild imperative -ón, which always draw prominence to the final syllable (pu'án, pu'ón); regular suffixes such as imperative -a do not. (iv) In spontaneous speech auxiliaries and clitics vary (tia, =cu, na= have no prominence; kó, 'ési, =káni, =kála do); a host+enclitic unit typically carries prominence on the host's last syllable (makasúa -> makasuá=cu), fn. 25: 'prominence position is often hard to predict' with clitics (pp. 86-88).
new_statements.identity_note: Cheng 2023 describes contemporary Kanakanavu as spoken in the Namasia District of Kaohsiung, based on a spontaneous-speech corpus, elicitation and a 241-verb database; it notes that the language's vowel system was restructured after the Ogawa and Asai (1935) documentation, so older transcriptions (Ogawa & Asai, Tsuchida 1976) mark stress on forms that differ segmentally from the modern ones.

tone_statements.quote: The data to be presented in Section 3 is strictly speaking Autosegmental-Metrical phonology (as it is from intonation rather than lexical tone) … In this model, the default intonational contour in Kanakanavu is one in which the f0 contour is entirely modulated by pitch accents (rather than boundary tones). The pitch accent is L+H*L, i.e. an f0 maximum aligned to the stressed syllable (H*), a pre-nuclear low tone (L) that spreads leftward from the syllable preceding stress, and a post-nuclear low tone that shifts rightward.
tone_statements.locator: p. 35 sec. 2.1 and p. 38 sec. 3.3 'Overview of intonational phonology'
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: pitch is intonational. Each word has a lexically determined stress (penult or antepenult) anchoring a post-lexical pitch accent L+H*L; enclitics take !H*L; a boundary H% marks topics.

tone_statements.quote: Stress in Kanakanavu has been described with the same acoustic cues as most other Formosan languages: a F0 peak, as well as increased duration and intensity. Interestingly, M. M. Y. Sung (1966) distinguishes between lexical items whose stressed syllable receives a pitch accent vs. those which don’t … I have not found such a distinction in word-stress as produced by Mu’u. Instead, I analyze variations in the magnitude of pitch accents as part of the intonational phonology … Kanakanavu’s intonational phonology can be described using the pitch accents L+H*L for stems and !H*L for clitics
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: pitch is intonational. An L+H*L pitch accent sits on the lexically stressed syllable, !H*L on enclitics, plus boundary tones H%, L%, %H; downstep is intonational (clitic !H, L%).

readall_conflicts: One disagreement of analysis type rather than placement: the catalog's existing statement (Cheng 2020, JSEALS SP5) is labelled weight-sensitive because it places prominence on the syllable carrying the underlyingly penultimate mora, while Cheng 2023 (same author, later work) explicitly denies weight sensitivity (p. 73) and recasts the rule as counting underlying vowels, with antepenultimate assignment in unsuffixed four-vowel words and penultimate otherwise. Both agree that prominence is predictable and penultimate by default with derived antepenult and final surface positions. Cheng 2023 also lists lexically prominence-specified stems, invariably antepenult reduplicated forms and two final-attracting suffixes, which the earlier statement summarises only as 'prominence-attracting/repelling affixes'. Older sources already held by the project (Sung 1966: penult or antepenult; Tsuchida 2003 and Li 2026: stress phonemic with low functional load; Wild 2018: penult, not distinctive) are compatible with the penult-default picture but differ on whether the placement is contrastive; Cheng 2023 treats it as rule-governed.

sources.note: p.16 §2.3.2 重音位置: '卡那卡那富語重音原則上落在詞的倒數第二音節，但也有不少詞彙重音節落在倒數第三音節上，如mamiriki「李子」[mamíriki]。當其詞根或詞幹加上前綴詞綴，一般而言，不會改變重音位置。但當其詞根或詞幹加上後綴詞綴時，重音有時不會移動，有時會往右移動一音節。' (stress in principle penultimate, but not a few words antepenultimate; prefixes do not move it; suffixes sometimes shift it one syllable rightward, e.g. matirupángʉ + -an -> matirupangáan). Refers readers to Chen (2016) [H. Chen NCNU MA thesis] for detail.

sources.note: p.799 §4 Stress and pitch: 'Most of the words in the Kanakanavu language comprise at least two syllables. In general, one of them is spoken with a greater degree of stress and a higher degree of pitch than the others. The stress of a word is always on the penult or third to the last syllable.. In words of four or more than four syllables, pitch always rises from the second syllable, and reaches its peak on the stressed syllable, then falls on the last syllables.' p.787: a stressed vowel is one and a half times longer.
